task.description: Step 1 (diagnose) of WF-03 for ISS-0418. Confirm or refute req170's mechanism against wasmex's real Rust source (installed wasmex ~> 0.15.1); enumerate where a concurrency cap can actually be enforced and assess each against whether it bounds LEAKED THREADS vs. merely concurrent CALLERS; determine whether the leak is bounded or unbounded in practice; reproduce cheaply if possible; state scope/routing. Do not implement a fix -- route to CODE-DESIGNER.

result.summary:
ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED, WITH ONE CORRECTION TO REQ170's MECHANISM NARRATIVE, AND LIVE-REPRODUCED ON THIS HOST. Full detail below; §7 states exactly what CODE-DESIGNER's design must decide.

=== 1. MECHANISM: CONFIRMED, with one correction ===

Read wasmex 0.15.1's real Rust source directly (mix.lock:24 confirms the installed version matches req170's verified version exactly -- no version drift). Files read in full: deps/wasmex/native/wasmex/src/{engine,store_executor,instance}.rs (paths relative to a worktree checkout of this same dependency tree -- .claude/worktrees/agent-a350015dab3f75408/deps/wasmex, same wasmex 0.15.1 per its own mix.lock).

CONFIRMED, verbatim from source:
  - engine.rs:8-20 -- TOKIO_RUNTIME is a `static ... LazyLock<tokio::runtime::Runtime>`, ONE runtime for the entire BEAM node, `worker_threads(available_parallelism())` (falls back to 8). This is genuinely node-global and shared across every wasmex Store/Engine in the process -- confirmed by there being exactly one `LazyLock` declaration in the whole native source tree (grep confirmed only two `TOKIO_RUNTIME.spawn` call sites total, both reusing this same static).
  - NOT CONFIGURABLE FROM THE BEAM SIDE AT ALL: grepped the full native/ and lib/ trees for `worker_threads`, `available_parallelism`, `WASMEX_*` env vars, and `Wasmex.EngineConfig`'s own fields (consume_fuel, wasm_backtrace_details, cranelift_opt_level, memory64, wasm_component_model, debug_info -- read directly from engine.rs's `ExEngineConfig` struct). None of them touch the Tokio runtime's thread count. The ONLY env var wasmex reads at all is `WASMEX_BUILD` (native.ex:27), which controls precompiled-vs-source NIF build, unrelated to runtime sizing. This matches req170 exactly -- no drift since 2026-08-28.
  - engine.rs's epoch-interruption setup (`config.epoch_interruption(true)`, a 10ms `EpochTicker` on the same shared runtime) and store_executor.rs's `with_deadline` (deadline race via `tokio::select!`, `interrupt_requested` flag) both exist in source exactly as req170 describes -- confirmed by reading them, not by trusting req170's quotes.

CORRECTION TO REQ170's MECHANISM NARRATIVE (a real finding, not nitpicking -- affects where a cap can bind): req170's prose describes 'once dispatched to wasmex's internal node-global Tokio worker pool, the guest runs forever' as if EACH INVOCATION spawns its own leaked task on the shared runtime. Reading store_executor.rs precisely shows the actual shape is ONE LEVEL MORE STRUCTURED than that: `StoreExecutor::with_capacity` (store_executor.rs:63-77) spawns exactly ONE long-lived Tokio task PER STORE (not per invocation) onto TOKIO_RUNTIME, which then does `while let Some(command) = receiver.recv().await { store = command(store).await; }` -- a single-threaded, ordered command queue for that Store's whole lifetime. `instance.rs:355` (`call_exported_function`) submits the guest call as one `command` into that queue via `executor.submit(...)`; the actual guest execution (`execute_function` -> `function.call_async(...).await`, instance.rs:383-417) runs inline inside that SAME per-Store task, awaited with `with_deadline` racing a `tokio::time::sleep_until(deadline)` (store_executor.rs:99-113). When the guest never yields at a working epoch checkpoint (req170 section 1.3's live-verified finding, unchanged), `with_deadline`'s `_ = future.await` on the timeout branch (store_executor.rs line ~109, `let _ = future.await;` inside the `sleep_until` arm) means the SAME per-Store task stays permanently blocked awaiting that non-yielding future -- it never returns to `recv().await`, so it can never dequeue another command either. So: it is NOT 'a fresh leaked task per invocation' in the sense of unbounded task count growing per call; it is exactly ONE leaked, permanently-blocked task PER Store-that-ever-received-a-hanging-call, and because `PluginHandler.start_instance/1` (plugin_handler.ex line ~171) creates a brand-new Store per invocation with no pooling (REQ-174 pooling explicitly declined, per plugin_handler.ex's own moduledoc), in THIS codebase's actual call pattern every hanging PluginInterface.invoke/2,3 call DOES produce a distinct new Store and therefore a distinct new permanently-blocked executor task -- so req170's operational conclusion (one leaked thread-equivalent per timed-out invocation, unbounded by call count) is still correct FOR THIS CALLER, but the mechanism is 'one blocked task per Store, and Letflow never reuses Stores' rather than 'one blocked task per raw invocation' as a NIF-level primitive. This distinction matters for design options that involve pooling/reusing Stores (see §2 below) -- reusing a Store across calls would NOT bound this leak (a single hang on a reused Store wedges that Store's queue forever, per store_executor.rs's ordered single-consumer design, matching req170 section 1.2's live 'permanently wedged Store' finding, now explained mechanistically), so Store-reuse is not a viable path to a fix, only a red herring worth naming so CODE-DESIGNER doesn't propose it.

A leaked task occupies one of the runtime's N worker OS threads whenever the Tokio scheduler has it polled and it never yields control back (`function.call_async` has no `spawn_blocking`/`block_in_place` -- confirmed absent by grep across instance.rs) -- so under Tokio's cooperative multi-thread scheduling, a non-yielding `.await` genuinely starves the worker thread it is running on, exactly as req170 claims, not merely 'occupies a queue slot with no real thread cost'. This is not asserted from reading alone -- §4 below reproduces it operationally.

=== 2. WHERE CAN A CAP ACTUALLY BE ENFORCED ===

Option A -- BEAM-side semaphore/counter (Letflow.Admission or a purpose-built equivalent) gating ENTRY to PluginHandler.run_guest/3 (i.e. before Wasmex.start_link/1 is even called): BOUNDS CONCURRENT CALLERS, DOES NOT BOUND LEAKED THREADS BY ITSELF. Read lib/letflow/admission.ex in full (REQ-216). It is a synchronous, non-queuing counting semaphore: try_acquire/2 (admission.ex line ~187) is a single GenServer.call that returns {:ok, ref} or {:error, :capacity} IMMEDIATELY, never parks a caller, and its own moduledoc states explicitly (the 'Crash / restart semantics' section) that it does NOT monitor callers -- 'a leaked ref stays counted against its budget until this process itself restarts or the ref is explicitly released.' This is the crux: Admission's release/2 must be called by the ref-holder for the budget to free up. If PluginHandler acquires a ref before dispatching a guest call and the guest hangs forever (the exact failure this cap exists for), the calling process is itself the one that would need to call release/2 -- and per PluginInterface.invoke/2,3's own existing algorithm (Task.Supervisor.async_nolink + Task.yield + Task.shutdown(:brutal_kill) on timeout), the task that acquired the ref is the one that gets brutally killed on the OUTER timeout, never running its own release/2 on that path. So a naive 'acquire on entry, release on completion' wiring would LEAK ADMISSION REFS AT EXACTLY THE SAME RATE AS THE UNDERLYING NATIVE LEAK -- Admission's own budget would itself permanently shrink to zero after enough hangs, same shape as the bug it exists to bound, just one layer up. This is fixable (acquire the ref in a process OUTSIDE the killed task -- e.g. the PluginInterface.invoke/2,3 caller itself, or a wrapper that guarantees release runs even if the inner task is brutal-killed, since release/2 does not require the SAME process that acquired -- Ref is a plain struct, not tied to caller pid) but it is a real design decision, not a mechanical wiring, and Letflow.Admission's own moduledoc never anticipated 'holder that can never call release because it was killed' as a scenario -- REVIEWER should check this against Admission's stated invariants before CODE-DESIGNER reuses it as-is. VERDICT: Admission (or an equivalent gate) bounds CONCURRENT CALLERS/invocations-in-flight at any moment, which is a real and valuable property (it prevents unbounded pile-up of simultaneous PluginHandler.run_guest/3 calls from launching more Stores than the operator wants at once) -- but it does NOT by itself reclaim or cap the count of PERMANENTLY LEAKED tasks already stuck in the Tokio pool, and if refs are never released for hung calls, admission slots for WASM calls asymptotically approach zero over time regardless of the cap's numeric value, which is the same failure mode restated one layer up unless the design explicitly accounts for never-released refs (e.g. a lease/lifetime bound independent of caller cooperation, which Admission's current design does not have).

Option B -- pool of pre-spawned wasmex Store/Instance processes with bounded checkout: DOES NOT WORK, for a mechanistic reason found in §1's corrected mechanism, not merely 'probably bad.' store_executor.rs's per-Store executor task processes ONE command at a time from an ordered mpsc queue and never abandons a stuck command (`store = command(store).await` -- the loop does not resume until that await resolves). Checking a Store back into a pool after a hang is not merely difficult, it's IMPOSSIBLE in the current wasmex API: there is no cancellation handle for an in-flight command (confirmed in §1 -- `with_deadline`'s timeout branch still `.await`s the stuck future), so a 'pooled' Store that ever receives one hang is permanently wedged and can never be checked back in -- pooling would only add bookkeeping overhead on top of the exact same unbounded-leak mechanism, with the added downside of falsely implying reuse is safe. REQ-174 (WASM-13, instance pooling) was already DECLINED per plugin_handler.ex's own moduledoc, citing 'no first-party wasmex pooling API exists' -- this option was correctly ruled out for unrelated reasons already, and this diagnosis independently confirms it would not solve THIS issue's mechanism either.

Option C -- configuring wasmex's own Tokio pool size: NOT REACHABLE AT ALL, confirmed in §1 above by direct grep across the full native and lib/ source trees -- there is no NIF parameter, env var, or `Wasmex.EngineConfig` field that touches `worker_threads`/`available_parallelism`. This is not a design option; it would require forking or patching the wasmex dependency itself, which is out of scope for an operator-configurable-cap fix and was not requested by ISS-0418's own title.

Option D -- other options found in source: (i) Running each WASM invocation in an OS SUBPROCESS (a la how CI's own `mix test --only wasm_hang` isolation already contains the damage to a short-lived process) would genuinely bound the leak's LIFETIME (the leaked thread dies when the subprocess is killed/exits) but is a much larger architectural change than 'a cap' -- effectively re-deriving what ISS-0352's OS-process isolation already does for CI, generalized to production traffic; almost certainly too large for this issue's own scope and probably its own requirement, but naming it because it is the only option found that bounds leaked-thread LIFETIME rather than merely rate. (ii) A supervisory watchdog that restarts the whole BEAM node once some leaked-task threshold is inferred (e.g. via a synthetic non-hanging probe call periodically checking pool health, mirroring this diagnosis's own probe technique in §4) would bound total accumulated damage by periodically paying the cost of a full node restart -- operationally heavyweight, but is the only mechanism found anywhere in this investigation that actually RECLAIMS the leaked resource (a node restart is the only thing wasmex's own architecture permits, per req170 section 1.4's finding that this is the sole documented recovery: 'It runs until it completes on its own (never, for this class of guest) or the whole BEAM node restarts.').

SUMMARY TABLE for CODE-DESIGNER: (A) BEAM semaphore on entry -- bounds concurrent callers/Stores-in-flight; does NOT reclaim leaked threads; must solve the 'never-released ref on brutal-kill' problem or it degrades to the same unbounded-leak shape one layer up. (B) Store pooling -- mechanistically ruled out, do not pursue. (C) Configure wasmex's pool size -- not reachable, not a real option. (D-i) subprocess-per-invocation -- bounds leak lifetime, likely too large for this issue's scope, name as a follow-up. (D-ii) periodic health-probe + node restart -- the only mechanism that reclaims already-leaked threads, heavyweight, worth naming as a complementary mitigation alongside (A) rather than a replacement for it.

=== 3. IS THE LEAK BOUNDED OR UNBOUNDED IN PRACTICE ===

UNBOUNDED IN PRACTICE, LIVE-CONFIRMED THIS SESSION (§4): after saturating the pool with schedulers_online()=16 concurrent hangs on this host, a subsequently-dispatched trivial non-hanging guest call did not return within 90,000ms of waiting (probe design allowed up to 90s specifically to test for recovery). No BEAM-side or wasmex-side mechanism reclaimed any of the 16 leaked tasks in that window. This matches req170 section 1.4's own conclusion ('no mechanism available from the BEAM side... can reach or terminate this already-dispatched native execution... it runs until it completes on its own (never, for this class of guest) or the whole BEAM node restarts') and extends it: this diagnosis affirmatively tested for recovery over a much longer window (90s vs. req170's own section 1.5 test, which only established stall within a 58s remaining budget) and found none. A cap that merely QUEUES new callers while leaked threads still accumulate is explicitly NOT a fix by this measure -- every additional hang under a queuing cap still permanently consumes one more of the N pool slots, so a busy tenant's WASM traffic over a long enough time window will still exhaust the pool even with perfect admission-control queuing, just more slowly. The only two things that change this conclusion are (D-i) killing the OS process the leaked thread lives in, or (D-ii) restarting the node -- both discussed in §2.

=== 4. REPRODUCTION (live, this host, this session) ===

Built two throwaway probes (WASMEX_BUILD=true MIX_ENV=test mix run <script>), both cleaned up afterward per scratch/ convention -- git status --porcelain confirms scratch/ is clean, nothing left behind.

Probe 1 (pool exhaustion): dispatched System.schedulers_online()=16 concurrent hanging guest calls (identical fixture shape to req165_hang.wat: `(loop $forever br $forever)`) each with wasmex's own 5000ms timeout, via Task.Supervisor.async_nolink mirroring PluginHandler's real call shape exactly. All 16 crashed/exited as expected (`** (stop) exited in: GenServer.call(..., {:call_function, "hang", [], 5000}, 5000) ** (EXIT) time out`, sixteen instances observed in log output). Two seconds after all 16 had already crashed, dispatched ONE trivial non-hanging guest (`(i32.const 42)`) with a 10,000ms timeout, waited up to 20,000ms via Task.yield. RESULT (quoted verbatim from real run output, reproduced twice for confidence): 'TRIVIAL CALL DID NOT RETURN within 20000ms -- POOL EXHAUSTION CONFIRMED'. Ran this probe twice; both runs produced the identical outcome.

Probe 2 (recovery window): same setup, but after saturating the pool, waited up to 90,000ms for the trivial call (instead of 20,000ms) to test whether the pool ever recovers given more time. RESULT (quoted verbatim): 'STILL EXHAUSTED after 90000ms -- no recovery observed'.

This directly and cheaply reproduces, on this exact host (16 logical CPUs, confirmed via `nproc`=16 matching `System.schedulers_online()`=16 in probe output), the same mechanism CI's isolated wasm_hang subprocess hits under contention on smaller/shared GitHub Actions runners -- the CI flake is the SAME mechanism at smaller/noisier scale, not a different one requiring separate diagnosis.

=== 5. SCOPE AND ROUTING ===

ISS-0352's test-only mitigation route (raised @tag timeout values, ISS-0406's mitigation) is CONFIRMED EXHAUSTED as evidence: ISS-0418's own recurrence log shows continued failures AFTER that mitigation shipped (recurrence_2026_09_03 through recurrence_2026_09_04_b, all postdating ISS-0406's 180_000ms @tag timeout fix), and this diagnosis's own reproduction shows WHY raising timeouts cannot fix this class -- the failure is resource exhaustion (pool has zero free slots), not insufficient wait time; waiting longer on an exhausted pool does not help (§3's 90s-recovery test empirically confirms this). Test-only mitigation is the wrong layer for this defect, confirmed rather than assumed.

THIS GOES TO CODE-DESIGNER. This is a genuine design decision, not a mechanical fix, matching the issue's own 'eight-plus deferrals' framing -- there is no single obviously-correct answer among §2's options, and Option A's most promising path (BEAM-side admission gating) has a real unresolved sub-problem (never-released refs on brutal-kill) that Letflow.Admission's existing design does not currently handle and that REVIEWER should sign off on before it's reused here unmodified.

WHAT THE DESIGN MUST DECIDE, explicitly, so CODE-DESIGNER does not have to re-diagnose:
  1. Whether to adopt Option A (admission gating on PluginHandler.run_guest/3 entry) as the primary mechanism, and if so, HOW release/2 is guaranteed to run even when the calling task is brutal-killed by PluginInterface.invoke/2,3's outer timeout (candidate: acquire the ref in the invoke/2,3 caller's own process, outside the killed inner task, and release it there once Task.yield/Task.shutdown resolves either way -- this needs a real design, not a one-line wiring, because Letflow.Admission was built for REQ-216's HTTP/poller admission use case where callers cooperate and release normally, not for a caller that can be involuntarily killed mid-hold).
  2. Whether to explicitly document (matching req170/call_timeout.ex's own precedent of stating divergences plainly rather than absorbing them) that Option A bounds CONCURRENT invocations-in-flight but does NOT reclaim already-leaked threads, and that the leak is confirmed unbounded over long time windows (§3) -- i.e. the cap is harm-REDUCTION (slows time-to-exhaustion, bounds worst-case simultaneous damage) not harm-ELIMINATION, unless paired with something from Option D.
  3. Whether a complementary mechanism from Option D (subprocess isolation generalized to production, or a periodic health-probe-triggered restart) is in this issue's scope or should be filed as a further follow-up issue -- this diagnosis recommends filing D as follow-up scope (name it explicitly, do not silently drop it) rather than blocking THIS fix on it, since Option A is independently valuable (bounds simultaneous damage and gives operators a real dial) even without D.
  4. The cap's own numeric default and configuration surface (operator-configurable, per the issue's own title) -- OQ-1-style question, not blocking, CODE-DESIGNER's normal discretion.
  5. Whether Letflow.Admission itself should be extended (a `:wasm` pool_selector variant, or a lease-with-timeout primitive) or whether a new, purpose-built, smaller semaphore is more appropriate given point 1's mismatch with Admission's current release-cooperation assumption -- REVIEWER-adjacent judgement call CODE-DESIGNER should make explicitly and justify, not silently default either way.

No defect found in Letflow.Admission's own REQ-216 scope -- it does exactly what its own design promises for its own intended callers (HTTP/poller, which do cooperate and always release). The mismatch is specific to reusing it for a caller that can be involuntarily killed mid-hold, which is a NEW property this issue's use case needs that REQ-216 never required.

Probes used: scratch/iss0418_pool_probe.exs, scratch/iss0418_recovery_probe.exs (both written, run, and deleted this session -- confirmed via `git status --porcelain`, scratch/ clean, no stray files). No production code under lib/letflow/engine/wasm/ or elsewhere was modified.
result.next_action: Route to CODE-DESIGNER for fix design per WF-03 Step 2. Design must resolve the five explicit decision points in result.summary section 5, particularly the never-released-Admission-ref-on-brutal-kill problem before reusing Letflow.Admission unmodified.
